## Parliament

The Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body of the Republic of India. It is a bicameral legislature composed of the President of India and the two houses: the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People). The President is not a member of either house but is an integral part of the Parliament.

Parliamentary sovereignty in India is subject to the Constitution, which establishes a judicial review mechanism through the Supreme Court. Unlike the British model of parliamentary supremacy, the Indian Parliament operates within the limits set by the fundamental rights and the federal structure.

### Rajya Sabha

The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of Parliament and represents the states and union territories of India. It is a permanent house that is not subject to dissolution. One-third of its members retire every two years, ensuring continuity of membership.

Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies using the method of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. The President of India nominates twelve members who have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service.

The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Deputy Chairman is elected from among the members of the house. The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250 members, of whom 238 are elected and 12 are nominated.

### Lok Sabha

The Lok Sabha is the lower house of Parliament and is composed of directly elected representatives of the people. It is the house of the people, with a maximum sanctioned strength of 552 members, including up to two members nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community and representatives of union territories.

The Lok Sabha is elected for a term of five years, which may be extended during a proclamation of emergency by Parliament. Its members are elected on the basis of universal adult franchise from territorial constituencies across the country.

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the proceedings of the house and is the guardian of its privileges. The Speaker is elected by the members of the house from among themselves, usually in the first session after a general election.

### Speaker of the Lok Sabha

The Speaker is the constitutional and ceremonial head of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker decides whether a bill is a money bill under Article 110, and that decision is final. The Speaker presides over joint sittings of the two houses, which are convened to resolve disagreements on ordinary legislation.

The Speaker does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie. The Speaker is expected to act impartially and to uphold the dignity and privileges of the house, even though the office is contested by the ruling party.

### Sessions of Parliament

Parliament normally meets in three sessions each year: the Budget Session, the Monsoon Session, and the Winter Session. The President summons each house of Parliament to meet at such time and place as the President thinks fit, with a maximum gap of six months between two sessions.

### Parliamentary Committees

Parliamentary committees examine legislation, scrutinize government expenditure, and oversee the administration of laws. The Public Accounts Committee, the Estimates Committee, and the Committee on Public Undertakings are the three financial committees of Parliament.

Departmentally related standing committees examine the demands for grants of the various ministries and report to the house. They strengthen parliamentary oversight of the executive by providing detailed scrutiny of policy and expenditure.
